idea: If AI takes the work juniors used to learn on, who trains the seniors you'll need in 2030?
flow: The bottom rung is going: at Anthropic, juniors fell from about one in four new technical hires to fewer than one in ten since early 2025, and a study of US firms finds junior hiring slowing where AI arrives.
We've been here before: cash machines and spreadsheets took the dull bottom of a job, and the job that was left got bigger.
What's different this time: AI takes the first draft itself, the work juniors learned on, and the cut is quiet because the junior job never opens.
Who trains your 2030 seniors: managers now hire for judgement, which people used to learn in their junior years.
His first rung: a junior at Microsoft in 2008, a half-million-row spreadsheet by hand, an Excel macro, and the lesson that came from the dull job.
ending: No prediction (Krish, 2026-10-26: "I think this one doesnt need a prediction"). His first rung, then the question for the next hiring meeting (who on this team will be a senior in 2030, and what are they learning on today), then a word to juniors.
takeaway: Before you cut a junior role, name who will be your 2030 senior and what real work they learn on today.
angle: The junior rung, past and future: earlier tools took the dull bottom of a job and the job came back bigger; this time AI takes the work juniors learned on.
tone: Observational, witty and positive; his own story told humbly, with the joke on himself.
reader: Leaders of medium-sized companies who sign off hiring.
agreed: Krish, 2026-10-27: "yes to all three, send fri and keep going"
